standard.title: Locate, select and compare information
standard.description: locate, select and compare information, data and ideas from a range of sources
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can locate, select and organise information, data and ideas from different sources (AC9HC8S02). At Year 9 the expectation advances from organising to comparing — students are expected to evaluate relative accuracy and reliability across sources, not just find and sort relevant information.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students locate, select and compare information, data and ideas from a range of sources, evaluating the accuracy and reliability of different sources.

nodes.label: Locating and selecting relevant information
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can locate information from a range of source types and select what is relevant to their inquiry.
nodes.minimum_width: Locate information on a civic, political or legal issue from at least two different source types (e.g. a government website and a news article) and select information relevant to the inquiry question.
nodes.typical_width: Locate information from a range of print and online source types — including statistics, graphs, tables, maps, articles, blogs and advertisements — and select relevant information or data about a civic issue; explain why some sources are more relevant than others for a specific inquiry question.
wider: Locate information from primary sources (e.g. parliamentary Hansard, legislation, court judgements) alongside secondary sources and compare what each type offers for civic inquiry
Investigate how to access government data sets or ABS statistics and use them to support analysis of a civic issue
Practise locating information on a contentious civic issue (e.g. water policy, COVID policy) across multiple source types and assess which source types are most informative

response_modes.reason: Students default to search engines and Wikipedia. Building familiarity with a wider repertoire of source types — government databases, Hansard, NGO reports, statistical data sets — is prerequisite to the comparative analysis in Node 2.

success_criteria: Locates information on a civic issue from at least two different source types
Identifies which information is most relevant to the inquiry question and explains the selection

nodes.label: Comparing accuracy and reliability across sources
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can compare sources and explain why some have greater accuracy and reliability than others for a given civic inquiry.
nodes.minimum_width: Compare two sources on the same civic issue and explain why one has greater accuracy or reliability than the other.
nodes.typical_width: Identify why some sources and information have greater accuracy and reliability than others; apply criteria such as authority, currency, bias, purpose, and evidence base to evaluate sources; compare across source types (e.g. government reports vs opinion pieces vs social media posts); explain how source reliability varies by inquiry question.
wider: Evaluate sources on a specific contested civic issue (e.g. Indigenous rights, refugee policy, climate legislation) where sources reflect strongly opposed perspectives, and assess how to use each appropriately
Investigate how misinformation circulates on civic topics and develop criteria for identifying unreliable sources in a social media context
Compare Australian and international sources on the same civic issue and evaluate how national context affects source perspective and reliability

response_modes.reason: Comparing source reliability is a reasoning task, not a checklist exercise. Students need explicit practice applying evaluative criteria to real source comparisons — particularly for sources where bias is subtle or where authority and motivation conflict.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Contested civic issues where multiple source types conflict (e.g. policy debates where government, NGO, and media accounts all diverge) are rich contexts for developing sophisticated source evaluation skills. This is a transferable capability with value well beyond Year 9 Civics.
success_criteria: Compares at least two sources on a civic issue and explains which is more reliable and why
Applies at least two evaluative criteria (e.g. authority, currency, bias, purpose) when comparing sources
